rules.title: A claim that appeals to what the reader knows
rules.text: `It is worth noting`, `Of course`, `Obviously`, `Needless to say`: the sentence tells the reader that a fact is already known or needs no argument, and then states it as though the audience had supplied the evidence. State the fact; drop the frame.

inspection.pattern: (?mi)(?:^|[ \t])(?:it(?:'|\u2019)s worth noting|it is worth noting|worth noting that|it (?:should|must) be noted|it(?:'|\u2019)s important to note|it is important to note|needless to say|as (?:we all|you) know|of course|obviously|it goes without saying)(?:[ \t]|[.,;:!?)])

judgement.question: Does this line frame a fact as obvious or already known instead of stating it?

criteria.true: the line hedges or appeals to shared knowledge (`it is worth noting`, `of course`, `obviously`, `needless to say`) in place of the fact or the measurement
criteria.false: the phrase is quoted or named in order to ban it, or the word is doing factual work (a test that is not obviously broken, a step the reader can in fact skip)
